section.title: Further Sayings of the Wise
section.sectionRationale: A short supplement follows the thirty sayings, explicitly introduced as 'also sayings of the wise,' 24:23, before the book moves into the Hezekiah collection in chapter 25. It presses on courtroom honesty and closes with a vivid, first-person parable of a lazy man's ruined field, learned by observation rather than command.
section.thesis: Honest judgment matters more than smooth partiality, and the ruin that overtakes a lazy man's field is a lesson meant to be watched, taken to heart, and heeded before poverty arrives like a robber.
section.frameNote: Two clusters: honest judgment versus partiality and flattery; the observed parable of the sluggard's ruined field and the poverty that follows a little more sleep.

verses.text: These also are sayings of the wise: To show partiality in judgment is not good.
Whoever tells the guilty, "You are innocent," peoples will curse him, and nations will denounce him;
but it will go well with those who convict the guilty, and rich blessing will come upon them.
An honest answer given is like a kiss on the lips.
Complete your outdoor work and prepare your field; after that, you may build your house.
Do not testify against your neighbor without cause, and do not deceive with your lips.
Do not say, "I will do to him as he has done to me; I will repay the man according to his work."
I went past the field of a {{atsel|slacker}} and by the vineyard of a man lacking judgment.
Thorns had grown up everywhere, thistles had covered the ground, and the stone wall was broken down.
I observed and took it to heart; I looked and received instruction:
A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest,
and poverty will come upon you like a robber, and need like a bandit.

atsel.gloss: Slacker, sluggard, one habitually averse to labor. Verse 30 pictures his field overrun with thorns and his wall broken down, a visible portrait of how small, repeated neglect compounds into visible ruin, a warning Proverbs repeats often, for example 6:6-11, almost word for word.

basic.context: This short supplement, explicitly labeled 'also sayings of the wise,' rounds off the longer collection before it. It insists that courts must convict the guilty rather than flatter them with false acquittal, and it closes with an unforgettable, first-person parable: the teacher walks past a neglected field, sees the ruin, and draws out the lesson that a little more sleep invites poverty like an armed robber.
basic.hermeneutics: This passage mixes direct commands, do not show partiality, do not testify falsely, with an observed parable rather than a command; the teacher does not simply state 'do not be lazy' but shows the ruin and lets the reader draw the conclusion, a method Scripture itself models as effective teaching through observation, not only through direct instruction.
basic.originalLanguages: The atsel, slacker or sluggard, verse 30, is a repeated character type in Proverbs, most memorably here and in 6:6-11, always pictured concretely, a ruined field, a broken wall, never abstractly. The phrase 'a little sleep, a little slumber,' verse 33, uses rhythmic repetition to mimic the slow, almost pleasant slide into ruin that laziness produces.
basic.typology: The call to convict the guilty rather than call them innocent, verse 24, anticipates the perfect justice of Christ's judgment, which never flatters sin but calls it what it is, even while offering mercy to those who repent. The ruined field observed and taken to heart, verses 30-34, anticipates the parables of Jesus, who likewise used observed, everyday pictures, seeds, soils, vineyards, to teach eternal lessons.
basic.christ: The insistence that whoever calls the guilty innocent will be cursed by peoples, verse 24, while blessing comes to those who convict the guilty, verse 25, anticipates the perfect justice of Christ, who never minimizes sin yet offers real mercy to those who confess it, holding justice and grace together at the cross in a way no human judge fully can. And the teacher's method of observed parable, walking past a field and drawing a lesson, verses 30-34, is the same teaching method Jesus later perfects, using ordinary fields and vineyards to reveal the kingdom of God.
basic.god: God's own justice stands behind the courtroom principle of this passage; calling the guilty innocent is a lie about reality itself, which God, the truthful judge, will not bless, while convicting the guilty rightly reflects His own character and draws real blessing. He is also patient enough to let ordinary consequences, a field gone to thorns, a wall fallen down, teach the lesson that direct command alone might not land.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 5:20 echoes the warning against calling evil good and good evil, as in verse 24. Matthew 13 shows Jesus teaching through observed agricultural parables like the one in verses 30-34. Proverbs 6:6-11 repeats the sluggard's ruin almost word for word. Galatians 6:7-9 echoes the certainty of consequence, sowing and reaping, behind the ruined field.
basic.oneStory: This short passage insists on honest justice in the courtroom and lets a ruined, thorn-choked field preach its own sermon about the slow creep of laziness into poverty. Both threads point toward Christ, the perfectly just judge who never calls evil good, and the master teacher who used ordinary fields to reveal eternal truth.

context.literary:
The heading in 24:23, 'These also are sayings of the wise,' works like a small colophon. It marks a second batch of wisdom sitting beside the thirty sayings, an appendix gathered by the same circle of teachers. The unit is short, but it has a clear internal design: five verses on speech and justice (24:23 to 29), then a first person narrative that carries the whole weight of the lesson (24:30 to 34).

The first half is a miniature on truthfulness. It begins with the courtroom, where partiality is condemned and a verdict that matches the facts is blessed, 24:23 to 25. It ends with the private world of neighbours: do not testify without cause, do not deceive with your lips, do not repay in kind, 24:28 to 29. In the middle sits a single image of honest speech as a kiss, 24:26, and an odd saying about order of work, 24:27. The courtroom and the field are thus linked by one theme: things should be done in the right order, and words should match what is so.

The second half changes voice. The earlier proverbs speak in the third person or command; here the teacher says 'I went past,' 'I observed,' 'I looked and received instruction,' 24:30 to 32. The parable is built from four brief movements: the sight (30 to 31), the reflection (32), the maxim (33) and the sentence (34). The maxim in 24:33 is lifted almost word for word from 6:10 to 11, so the book hears itself, and the repeated lines act like a refrain that the reader now knows by heart.

The unit also closes a larger movement. The words of the wise run from 22:17 to here, and the next verse, 25:1, opens a new collection with a new heading. The placing of the sluggard's field at this threshold gives the reader a last picture before the book turns to the proverbs of Hezekiah's men.
context.historical:
The scene is rural, and its details would have been plain to anyone raised in Judah. A vineyard sat on terraced hillside and was enclosed by a wall of fieldstone, which kept out animals and marked the owner's rights. Such a wall needed yearly care: winter rains dislodged stones, and a gap let in goats and thieves. Thorns and thistles overrunning a plot were the clearest sign that nobody had worked it for a season or two, as Isaiah's vineyard song shows when the owner abandons his vineyard to briers, Isaiah 5:5 to 6.

The order given in 24:27 reflects the economy of a peasant household. The first duty was the food supply, the outdoor work and the field. A house, whether the building or the household of marriage and children, came afterwards, and only when the fields could support it. The teacher is not despising family life; he is saying that a young man should secure his livelihood before taking on what he cannot yet feed. Jesus tells a similar story of the builder who counts the cost, Luke 14:28.

The courtroom saying belongs to the town gate. Judges were elders sitting in public view, and a case was decided on the evidence of witnesses, Deuteronomy 19:15. The Torah warned judges against favouring either rich or poor, Deuteronomy 1:17, and the whole system depended on witnesses who told the truth, since a false witness could ruin a neighbour with no recourse. This is why a verdict of innocence over the guilty draws a curse from 'peoples' and 'nations' in the saying: a society that cannot trust its courts loses its people's confidence.

The phrase 'the men of Hezekiah' in the next verse suggests that these collections were preserved and arranged in the royal court centuries after Solomon, so a short supplement like this could have been included within a longer collection that scribes had already received. The mention of a teacher walking past a field is a reminder that Israel's wise men learned by looking at the world, not only at books.
context.canonical:
The courtroom principle comes straight from the Torah. The judge is to 'show no partiality,' Deuteronomy 1:17, and the identical idiom reappears in Proverbs 28:21. Proverbs 17:15 names the reverse offence as 'detestable to the LORD': acquitting the guilty and condemning the righteous. Isaiah calls down woe on those who call evil good, Isaiah 5:20, a line that shows the same value working at the level of a nation's moral vision. Paul's statement that 'God does not show favoritism,' Romans 2:11, and Peter's confession in Acts 10:34 present this justice as a trait of God Himself.

The ban on repaying a wrong in kind is repeated in 20:22, 'Do not say, I will avenge this evil! Wait on the LORD.' The New Testament takes it up in Romans 12:17 and 1 Peter 3:9, where the believer is told to bless instead of retaliating. The sluggard's field is the best known case of a motif that runs through the book, 6:6 to 11, 10:4, 13:4, 20:4, and out into the New Testament as Paul's command that those who will not work should not eat, 2 Thessalonians 3:10, and his instruction that the former thief should labour with his hands so that he has something to share, Ephesians 4:28.

The ruined field also joins the large biblical picture of land that returns to thorns when its keepers fail. After the fall the ground yields 'thorns and thistles,' Genesis 3:18, and Hebrews 6:8 uses the same phrase to describe land that bears nothing useful. Isaiah's vineyard becomes a wasteland of briers when the vines produce sour fruit, Isaiah 5:6, and Jesus declares Himself the 'true vine' whose Father tends the vineyard, John 15:1. The supplement thus touches some of the Bible's most important recurring images.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The teacher's main aim in the first half was to protect the integrity of speech in public life. The courtroom saying is not about legal theory; it is a warning to young men who might one day sit on a town's bench or give testimony before it. Convicting the guilty and refusing favouritism will not always make a man popular, but the proverb says it will bring blessing, and false acquittal will bring a curse from peoples and nations. The same sage who values an 'honest answer' as a mark of affection, 24:26, wants his pupil to treat truth as a form of love.

The second half is where the teacher's method becomes visible. He does not preach at the sluggard. He tells a story of his own walk, shows the wreck, and says that he 'took it to heart.' The first hearers were meant to put themselves in the teacher's shoes, to look at someone else's ruin and let it speak to their own habits. The final verse is deliberately gentle in its pace and sharp in its edge: the slide into ruin comes in small, comfortable steps, and the arrival is sudden, like a robber at the door.

The intended response is practical. Do not give a verdict to please; do not speak against a neighbour for no cause; do not store up a private score; and above all, do not treat a little extra rest as harmless when work is waiting. The saying about order, 24:27, adds a quiet corrective for a young man's plans: secure the field before furnishing the house.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The first section is mostly prescriptive, because the commands rest on the Torah's justice and on the character of God. A judge must not favour the guilty, a witness must not deceive, and a person must not pursue private revenge. These are binding moral obligations, and the later Scriptures confirm them.

The parable is of a different kind. It describes what the teacher saw and what usually follows from habitual idleness. It does not command anyone to build walls or keep a certain schedule, and it does not state that everyone who is poor is lazy. The book itself says that abundant food may lie in the fallow ground of the poor, but without justice it is swept away, 13:23, and that rich and poor share the same Maker, 22:2. The right use of the parable is therefore to examine one's own habits, not to diagnose others. A believer applies it by asking where small delays and comfortable postponements are quietly wrecking a field he is responsible for, whether that is a job, a marriage, a body or a soul. The word of Paul to the idle, 2 Thessalonians 3:10, is addressed to those who can work and will not, not to those who cannot.

debates.question: Does the sluggard's field teach that poverty is always the result of laziness?

views.label: Poverty is usually self inflicted
views.case: The parable and its relatives, 6:6 to 11, 10:4 and 13:4, link idleness to want, and the teacher states a direct cause: little sleep leads to poverty. On this view the book's wisdom is that effort and prudence normally produce provision, and the exceptions do not cancel the rule.

views.label: Poverty has many causes, and Proverbs knows it
views.case: Other sayings in the same book show poverty from injustice, 13:23, from oppression, 22:22 and from simple unequal circumstances under one Maker, 22:2. Job and the prophets also describe the righteous poor. The sluggard saying addresses one cause, not all of them.

debates.bearing: Both are right when each is kept in its place. The parable is a warning to the one holding the hoe, not a verdict on the person at the gate. Used as a lens on others, it becomes the cruelty the rest of Proverbs condemns; used as a mirror, it is exactly what the teacher intends.

debates.question: What does 'build your house' mean in 24:27?

views.label: Establish a livelihood before a household
views.case: The 'house' is the household of marriage and children. The saying advises a young man to prepare the field, which supplies food, before taking on a family. This reading fits the agricultural order and the wise man's concern for stability.

views.label: Do the necessary work before the comfortable
views.case: A plainer reading takes 'house' as the building. The sage is saying that the work that feeds you comes before the work that shelters you, a general rule about priorities in the use of time and strength.

debates.bearing: The two readings differ in detail but share the point: order matters, and the urgent, productive task should come before the pleasant, deferrable one. Either reading rebukes a person who builds a showpiece while the field lies bare.

study.originalLanguages:
Four phrases in this short unit carry more than the English suggests. The first is the idiom of 24:23. 'To show partiality' is literally to recognise faces, and it appears in the same form in the law for judges in Deuteronomy 1:17 and in Proverbs 28:21. The judge is to be blind to who stands before him. The expression is not about malice but about familiarity: to look at the face is to be swayed by what the face stands for.

Second is the word for 'honest answer' in 24:26, which uses the plural of the common word davar, 'word' or 'matter.' The line pictures 'straight' or 'right' words given back to a questioner. The kiss in the simile is a kiss on the lips, a sign of loyalty and closeness. The writer is saying that a plain, true reply is a mark of affection in the same way a kiss is, because only someone who cares will risk the discomfort of telling the truth. The sad counterpart is the kiss of Judas, Matthew 26:48 to 49, a sign of friendship used to carry a lie.

Third is the description of the field's owner in 24:30. The BSB calls him one 'lacking judgment,' and the Hebrew is literally 'lacking heart,' chaser lev. In Hebrew thought the heart is the seat of understanding and decision, so the lack is of sense, not of kindness. The same phrase is used elsewhere in Proverbs of the simple young man who walks into a trap, 7:7. The sluggard, atsel, is therefore described by both his habit and his deficiency: he does not use his mind.

Fourth is the closing line of 24:34. The BSB renders the two figures as 'a robber' and 'a bandit.' The first word is a participle meaning one who walks about, a roving man. The second is understood by most translators as an armed man, and the Hebrew is literally a man of a shield. The thought is that poverty does not creep like a thief at night but strides in like a raider. The verse repeats 6:11 almost to the letter, so the book makes the point twice.

The verbs of 24:32, 'I observed and took it to heart; I looked and received instruction,' are worth reading slowly. 'Took it to heart' is literally set my heart, and the 'instruction' is musar, the discipline that has run all through the previous section. The wise man learns his discipline from a field, not only from a father. The folding of the hands in 24:33 is a gesture mentioned also in Ecclesiastes 4:5, 'The fool folds his hands and consumes his own flesh.'

typology.type: The faithful witness who convicts, Proverbs 24:24 to 26
typology.fulfillment: The judge who calls the guilty innocent is cursed, and the one who answers honestly is blessed. Christ is the perfect judge: 'with righteousness He will judge the poor, and with equity He will decide for the lowly of the earth,' Isaiah 11:4, and He is 'the faithful and true Witness,' Revelation 3:14. He told Pilate that He came 'to testify to the truth,' John 18:37. The correspondence rises because He does not merely tell the truth about sin; He bears its penalty, so that the verdict of guilt and the offer of mercy are held together. The type falls short because human judges cannot do this, and their honesty can only call the guilty guilty.

typology.type: The honest kiss and the betrayer's kiss, Proverbs 24:26
typology.fulfillment: The sage prizes the plain word as a true kiss, a mark of friendship that costs something. Judas used the kiss as a signal to hand Jesus over, Matthew 26:48 to 49, and the contrast stings: the outward sign of affection was the vehicle of treachery. Jesus answered him with a question that cut through, 'Judas, are you betraying the Son of Man with a kiss?' Luke 22:48. Christ Himself is the one who speaks straight words to His friends, John 15:15, and who heals even those who cut them. The type here works by contrast, and it falls short if pressed for more.

The overgrown plot echoes Isaiah's song of the vineyard that yielded sour fruit and was left to briers, Isaiah 5:1 to 6. There the owner is God and the vineyard is Israel. Jesus takes up the image as the true vine, John 15:1, in whom branches bear fruit, and warns that unfruitful branches are cut away, John 15:2. The sluggard's ruin therefore points to a fruitless people and, beyond them, to the One who bears fruit for them. The type falls short because the field here is a human plot, while the vineyard of Isaiah and John is the people of God, planted and tended by the Father.

typology.type: Thorns and thistles on the neglected ground, Proverbs 24:31
typology.fulfillment: The ground that the sluggard has let go yields 'thorns' and 'thistles,' the same pair that the curse promised in Genesis 3:18. Christ entered that curse: soldiers twisted a crown of thorns and pressed it on His head, Matthew 27:29, and Paul says He became a curse for us, Galatians 3:13. The correspondence escalates from a farmer's loss to a Saviour's wound. Where the sluggard's plot shows the effect of neglect, the cross shows God's own answer to the cursed ground. The type falls short because the proverb is about ordinary diligence, not atonement, and does not itself speak of Christ.

study.christ:
This small unit leads to Christ in several ways, and the first is by contrast. The sage commends the answer that cuts straight, the verdict that matches the facts, the witness that does not lie. Jesus is the full measure of that standard. He is 'the faithful and true Witness,' Revelation 3:14, and He came into the world 'to testify to the truth,' John 18:37. He was also falsely accused by witnesses whose words did not agree, Mark 14:55 to 59, so the one who embodies honest testimony was killed on the strength of dishonest testimony. The proverb's curse on false acquittal and its blessing on honest conviction are then answered in Him in an unexpected way: God does not call the guilty innocent by ignoring their guilt. He declares sinners righteous because the verdict fell on His Son, Romans 3:25 to 26.

Second, the unit leads to Christ by the shape of a refusal. The sage says 'Do not say, I will do to him as he has done to me,' 24:29. At the cross the Lord who could have called down legions did not repay, and 'when they hurled insults at Him, He did not retaliate,' 1 Peter 2:23. His prayer, 'Father, forgive them,' Luke 23:34, is the proverb lived to its end. This is more than an example. His refusal to retaliate is the reason that the sinner may be spared what he has earned.

Third, the field. The picture of the ruined vineyard sits near one of the Bible's greatest images. In Isaiah the vineyard is Israel, abandoned to thorns because it produced sour grapes, Isaiah 5:1 to 6. In John, Jesus says 'I am the true vine,' John 15:1, and the true vine does what the old vine failed to do. The failure of Israel's keeping, which the sluggard's field pictures in miniature, is met by a keeper who does not sleep and a vine that does not fail. It is also worth saying that Jesus was never idle. His rest in the boat was real, but His labour was constant, John 9:4, and He calls His followers to the work of the kingdom.

Fourth, the parable method itself belongs to Him. The teacher looks at an ordinary field and finds a lesson. Jesus does the same with seeds, soils, vineyards and barns, and He calls Himself the one greater than Solomon, Matthew 12:42, since in Him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, Colossians 2:3.

A word of care: the field is not a puzzle for coded Christology. The sluggard is not a figure for Christ, nor are the thorns a hidden reference to the cross by themselves. The links are those the New Testament itself draws, through the curse of Genesis 3:18, the vineyard of Isaiah 5 and the vine of John 15.
study.god:
The first thing the unit shows about God is that He is the judge whose character stands behind the courtroom. A verdict that calls the guilty innocent is not merely a legal error but a lie about the world, and God is the one who will not call evil good, Isaiah 5:20, and who finds acquittal of the guilty and condemnation of the innocent 'detestable,' 17:15. Peoples and nations curse the unjust judge because they live in the created order He established, in which justice is built into how a community holds together.

He is impartial. The Torah's rule that a judge must not show partiality is grounded in the statement that 'judgment belongs to God,' Deuteronomy 1:17, and Paul says God Himself 'does not show favoritism,' Romans 2:11. This impartiality is not coldness. It is what makes mercy trustworthy, because a God who could be bought could not be relied on to protect the weak.

He is a God of truth in speech. The proverb values the honest answer as a mark of love, which is consistent with a God who 'does not lie,' Titus 1:2, and who speaks truth to those whom He loves. He also forbids false testimony without cause, 24:28, because words are among the deeds for which He holds people accountable.

He is patient enough to let consequences teach. The field is not struck down by a sudden curse. It fails by degrees, through the slow outworking of the way He made the world to run. Poverty arrives 'like a robber,' not as a sentence but as a result. That is a kind of mercy, because it gives the sluggard time to see the ruin and change course, as the wise man did on his walk. The same patience marks the Lord's dealings in the prophets, who point to a failing vineyard while still calling for a return.

He is also the God who owns the work. A farmer's labour is not a merely worldly matter. The ground is the Lord's, Psalm 24:1, and diligence in it is a form of stewardship. Worship in the light of this passage means asking Him for an honest tongue, a just heart and a willingness to learn from what we pass by. It also means trusting Him in the matter of revenge, as the counterpart proverb says, 'Wait on the LORD, and He will save you,' 20:22, because He sees and will deal with wrongs, and we need not take the bench into our own hands.

crossReferences.note: Moses charges Israel's judges to show no partiality, to hear small and great alike, and to fear no one because judgment belongs to God. This is the legal root of 24:23 and gives the reason why a verdict must follow the facts: the judge sits under a higher Judge.

Acquitting the guilty and condemning the righteous are both detestable to the LORD. It sits as the sharper twin of 24:24 to 25: where this passage speaks of public curses and blessings, this verse names the divine verdict on a crooked court.

Woe to those who call evil good and good evil. The prophet turns the courtroom principle of 24:24 into a charge against a whole society whose moral language has been reversed, and shows how a false verdict becomes a false worldview.

The earlier sluggard passage that 24:33 to 34 repeats almost word for word. There the ant is the model of diligence, here a ruined field is the warning. Reading the two together shows how the book teaches the same lesson by a bright example and by a dark one.

The song of the vineyard describes a well tended plot that yielded sour fruit and was left to briers and drought. It uses the same field imagery as 24:30 to 31, but the owner is God and the vineyard is His people, which lifts the sluggard's field into a picture of national failure.

After the fall the ground brings forth thorns and thistles. The same pair covers the sluggard's vineyard in 24:31. The neglected field is therefore a small replay of the curse, showing what happens when human labour withdraws from a world already marked by the fall.

Paul tells believers not to repay evil for evil and to leave room for God's wrath. It lines up with the refusal of private vengeance in 24:29 and gives the New Testament reason: vengeance belongs to the Lord, and His people overcome by doing good.

Paul's rule that one unwilling to work should not eat, and his call for the idle to earn their own living, apply the lesson of 24:33 to 34 in the church. He addresses the unwilling, not the unable, and he asks them to work quietly.

The master calls the servant who hid his talent 'wicked' and 'lazy.' It shows that the Bible's judgment on idleness reaches beyond fields and into stewardship of what the Lord entrusts, so that the sluggard's loss becomes a picture of a spiritual failure to use what has been given.

Jesus is the true vine and the Father the keeper of the vineyard. The abandoned vineyard of Proverbs 24 finds its answer here, where the vine does not fail and the Father prunes, so that fruit is borne to the end.

study.oneStory:
The supplement is small, but it sits on one of the Bible's main roads. Humanity began as the keeper of a garden, given work to do before the fall, Genesis 2:15. After the fall the ground fights back with thorns and thistles, and labour becomes toil. The sluggard's field in Proverbs 24 is a snapshot of that world: a plot that was meant to be tended and has been left to the curse. It sets alongside the courtroom, where truth is also meant to be tended and can be abandoned. Together they show the two places where a fallen people most need wisdom, the shared life of the gate and the private life of the field.

The story presses forward from here. Israel was a vineyard planted by God, Isaiah 5:1 to 2, and the nation's failure to bear fruit ended in exile and ruin. The kings who sat in judgment too often favoured the powerful, and the prophets thundered against crooked courts. The proverb that blesses the honest judge and curses the corrupt one looks forward to a ruler who will judge the poor with righteousness, Isaiah 11:4, and a vine that will bear what the old vine did not, John 15:1.

Christ meets both needs. As the faithful witness and righteous judge He holds truth and mercy together. As the true vine, He is the keeper's perfect son in the vineyard. His people are then called to the same two tasks in the new life: to tell the truth in love, Ephesians 4:25, and to work with their hands and so have something to share, Ephesians 4:28. The slow slide the teacher saw in the field is answered by a life lived in the power of the Spirit.

The new creation completes the movement. The curse on the ground is removed, Revelation 22:3, and the thorns are gone. The river and the tree of life stand in a city where nothing false enters, Revelation 21:27, and where the Judge is also the Lamb. In that world no one's field falls into ruin, and the honest answer is the only kind there is.

quiz.q: What does verse 24 say happens to whoever tells the guilty 'you are innocent'?

options.text: Peoples will curse him, and nations will denounce him.
options.note: False acquittal draws widespread condemnation, not mere private disapproval.

options.text: He is rewarded with rich blessing.
options.note: That blessing belongs instead to those who rightly convict the guilty, verse 25.

options.text: He faces no consequence at all.
options.note: The verse specifically describes serious social consequence.

options.text: He is mildly criticized but ultimately respected.
options.note: The verse's language, cursed and denounced by peoples and nations, is far stronger than mild criticism.

options.text: "I will do to him as he has done to me; I will repay the man according to his work."
options.note: Personal vengeance dressed up as fairness is exactly what this verse forbids.

options.text: "I forgive you completely."
options.note: This is the opposite of what the verse actually forbids.

options.text: "I will help you regardless of what you have done."
options.note: This is not the statement the verse addresses.

options.text: "I will let the courts decide this matter."
options.note: This statement is closer to the verse's implied alternative, lawful process, rather than the forbidden statement itself.

quiz.q: What did the teacher observe when passing the sluggard's field, verse 31?

options.text: Thorns had grown up everywhere, thistles covered the ground, and the stone wall was broken down.
options.note: Visible, compounding neglect marks the field's ruin.

options.text: A thriving vineyard well cared for.
options.note: This is the opposite of the neglect the teacher actually observed.

options.text: An empty field with no crops planted at all.
options.note: The text specifically describes overgrowth and ruin, not mere emptiness.

options.text: A field partially maintained but with a few weeds.
options.note: The description is far more severe, thorns everywhere and a broken wall, than a few weeds.

quiz.q: According to verses 33-34, what does 'a little sleep, a little slumber' lead to?

options.text: Poverty coming like a robber, and need like a bandit.
options.note: Small, repeated laziness compounds into sudden, forceful poverty.

options.text: Restored strength and better productivity.
options.note: This is the opposite outcome described in the verses.

options.text: No real consequence, since rest is always beneficial.
options.note: The text specifically warns of serious consequence, not neutrality.

options.text: A gradual, gentle decline that is easily reversed.
options.note: The imagery of a robber and bandit suggests sudden, forceful loss, not a gentle, easily reversed decline.

quiz.q: What method does the teacher use to convey the lesson of verses 30-34?

options.text: A first-person observed parable, walking past a ruined field and drawing out its lesson.
options.note: The teacher shows rather than merely commands, letting observation teach the point.

options.text: A direct legal command with a stated penalty.
options.note: This is not the form used; it is observation and reflection, not legal command.

options.text: A dialogue between two named characters.
options.note: The passage is first-person narration of observation, not a dialogue.

options.text: A quotation from an ancient king.
options.note: There is no royal quotation here; it is the teacher's own personal observation.

questions: Verses 24-25 warn against calling the guilty innocent for the sake of comfort or approval. Where are you tempted to excuse wrongdoing, in yourself or someone close to you, rather than naming it honestly?
Verse 29 forbids repaying evil for evil under the guise of fairness. Is there someone you are quietly keeping score against, waiting for a chance to even things out?
The teacher observed a ruined field and 'took it to heart,' verse 32. What small area of neglect in your own life, if you are honest, is slowly turning to thorns?
'A little sleep, a little slumber' pictures how gradual small compromises become large ruin, verse 33. What small daily habit of yours needs correcting before it compounds further?
The whole passage rewards honest speech and honest labor. Where is God calling you to greater honesty this week, whether in words, work, or both?

translationNotes.note: 'An honest answer given is like a kiss on the lips' pictures the intimacy and warmth of truthful speech, a striking image for how valuable candor is between people.
'A man lacking judgment' translates a phrase describing someone devoid of sense or heart, chasar leb, the same root used elsewhere in Proverbs for those who lack basic discernment.
These two verses repeat 6:10-11 nearly verbatim, a deliberate echo showing the sluggard's ruin was proverbial enough to be quoted twice in the book.
